questions.stem: A neurotransmitter is released at a synapse and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neurone, triggering a new impulse. A drug is designed to block these receptors. What effect would this drug have?

options.text: It would speed up impulse transmission across the synapse
It would prevent the impulse from crossing the synapse to the next neurone
It would cause the neurotransmitter to travel backwards
It would increase the production of neurotransmitter

questions.explanation: If receptors on the postsynaptic membrane are blocked, the neurotransmitter cannot bind and trigger a new impulse. The signal would stop at the synapse. Many medications and poisons work by blocking synaptic receptors (e.g., some anaesthetics block pain signal transmission).

questions.stem: At a synapse, neurotransmitter molecules are stored in vesicles at the presynaptic terminal. When an impulse arrives, these vesicles fuse with the membrane and release their contents. Which cellular process is this most similar to?

options.text: Osmosis — movement of water across a membrane
Exocytosis — vesicles fusing with the cell membrane to release their contents
Diffusion — random movement of molecules down a concentration gradient
Endocytosis — the membrane folding inward to take in substances

questions.explanation: The release of neurotransmitter is an example of exocytosis — vesicles move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft. This process requires energy (ATP) and calcium ions to trigger it.

questions.stem: Synapses ensure that nerve impulses travel in only one direction. Why is this unidirectional transmission important?

options.text: It prevents impulses from reaching the brain too quickly
It ensures signals follow the correct pathway from receptor to effector, producing coordinated responses
It allows all neurones to fire at the same time
It is not important; impulses can travel in both directions

questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter vesicles are only on the presynaptic side, and receptors only on the postsynaptic side. This ensures impulses travel in one direction: from receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. This prevents confusion and ensures coordinated responses.

questions.stem: After a neurotransmitter has triggered an impulse in the postsynaptic neurone, it is quickly broken down by enzymes in the synaptic cleft. Why is this rapid removal necessary?

options.text: To recycle the neurotransmitter molecules for use in other parts of the body
To prevent continuous stimulation of the postsynaptic neurone, allowing the synapse to be ready for the next impulse
To generate additional energy for the neurone
To convert the neurotransmitter into myelin

questions.explanation: If neurotransmitter remained in the cleft, it would continuously stimulate the postsynaptic neurone, causing an uncontrolled response. Rapid enzymatic breakdown (or reuptake) clears the cleft, stopping the signal and resetting the synapse so it can transmit the next impulse accurately.

questions.stem: A nerve gas works by preventing the breakdown of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at synapses in muscles. What symptoms would exposure to this nerve gas cause?

options.text: Complete muscle relaxation and paralysis due to blocked impulses
Uncontrolled muscle contraction and spasms due to continuous stimulation
Loss of sensation but normal muscle function
Enhanced athletic performance due to stronger nerve signals

questions.explanation: If acetylcholine is not broken down, it continuously stimulates the postsynaptic membrane at neuromuscular junctions, causing muscles to contract uncontrollably. This leads to spasms, and if respiratory muscles are affected, it can be fatal. This is how some nerve agents and pesticides work.
